prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands at a magic angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in moire flat-band matter.

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a rare case in which a compact, controllable continuum model (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011) made a sharp quantitative prediction, a flat band at a magic twist angle, and experiments seven years later (Jarillo-Herrero and collaborators, 2018) found correlated insulators and superconductivity at that angle. From my own standpoint in electronic-structure theory, the interest is that interaction strength becomes a tunable geometric knob, so correlated physics that conventional DFT handles poorly can be explored systematically. The discovery has been reproduced by many independent groups across twisted multilayers and other moire materials. It has built a new field, and the theory-plus-experiment split into three names is natural.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity. The origin of the superconductivity is unsettled, the phase diagram depends on the sample, and the field is only about eight years old. A committee that prefers a stable interpretation could reasonably wait. There is also an attribution problem: the experimental credit sits with a group, and the first-author junior researcher and the groups that developed hBN-encapsulated devices (Dean and others) are not on the credited list. If the committee judged the field too young, the cold-atom Hubbard-simulation work (B001) is the more settled alternative.

responses.point: Olsson ranked B041 first, valuing that the effect is controlled by a geometric parameter in an engineered interface, and noted that junior experimental co-authors are not in the credited names.
responses.response: I agree on the engineered-interface point; it is also why I rank it first. I would go further than she does on attribution. The missing first-author experimentalist is a fairness problem that the shortlist cannot repair, and it weakens the case for a prize this year. I still think the three credited people are the only configuration the shortlist supports, and I do not think the gap should stop us.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Higgs discovery (B020) first as exceptional in importance, clarity and maturity, while noting the structural difficulty of crediting collaborations through a three-person limit.
responses.response: I do not dispute the importance of the Higgs discovery, and it is outside my subfield. My disagreement is about what is deliverable. His own attribution paragraph concedes that the ATLAS/CMS balance is not resolved, and four credited names compete for three seats. Mehlig makes the same point about CMS being thinly represented in a trio. A prize that is scientifically overwhelming but whose credit is arbitrary is, to me, a weaker candidate this year than one with a clean theory-plus-experiment split, even if the latter is younger.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B001 first, as a clear and mature experimental platform for Hubbard-type models, and ranks B041 second with a note that the unsettled pairing mechanism argues for a modest wait.
responses.response: I take the maturity point seriously and it is the main reason I hold B001 as my first alternative. Where I differ is that I do not think a settled superconducting mechanism is the right bar. The prize-worthy discovery is the flat-band prediction and the observation of correlated phases at the predicted angle, and both are robust whatever the pairing mechanism turns out to be. I also note that B001 has its own unresolved cut among five names (Zoller and Cirac against Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger), so it is not cleaner on attribution.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B041 last among his eight, judging it outside his field, rapidly replicated but possibly early, and notes that the pairing mechanism is incomplete.
responses.response: I accept that the timing concern is legitimate and I share it in part. I would answer that early replication across many labs and materials, which he acknowledges, is the evidence that the core result is robust, and the pairing question concerns a derived phase, not the discovery of the flat band and correlated insulators. His assessment is also, by his own account, made outside his expertise, so I weigh it less on the science than on the timing question.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the unresolved superconducting pairing mechanism as disqualifying for now or only as an open question within a durable field.
How to weigh the absence of the first-author experimentalist and of the hBN device groups from the credited names.
Whether a prize in 2026 would be perceived as overlapping with the 2016 topological-phases prize, a point I judge weak but cannot dismiss.
My own assessment of the cold-atom and clock candidates is outside my expertise and rests on general knowledge.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B041, B001 or B013. My work is in electronic-structure theory and magnetism at Uppsala, with no documented connection to the credited moire, cold-atom or clock researchers. My general interest in correlated-electron physics is a scientific bias I disclose, not a personal connection.
